A CASE OF UNDIAGNOSED STIFF-PERSON
SYNDROME REQUIRING MECHANICAL
VENTILATORY SUPPORT
Mayer, Neil; Kretzer, Adam; John, Sayona; Bleck, Thomas; Garg, Rajeev
Author Information
Critical Care Medicine 40(12):p 1-328, December
2012. | DOI: 10.1097/01.ccm.0000425359.78888.40
Metrics
Abstract
Case Reports:
We present a case of undiagnosed Stiff-Person Syndrome (SPS) requiring mechanical
ventilation due to high dose sedatives for antispasticity therapy. A 38 year-old women was
transferred from an outside hospital for further diagnostic evaluation and treatment of acute
onset “myoclonus.” Her history was remarkable for a several year decline in functional status
due to intermittent back spasms causing pain and limited mobility. She returned to the other
hospital after experiencing worsening spasms and wound breakdown from a total abdominal
hysterectomy performed one week earlier for dysfunctional uterine bleeding. She had a
wound infection and small bowel obstruction necessitating exploratory laparotomy with
bowel resection. Her back spasms progressively worsened post-operatively leading to painful
episodes of tachycardia, intermittent fevers, and severe “myoclonic jerks.” She was later
intubated and placed on a propofol infusion for concerns of status epilepticus. Differential
diagnosis and treatment included neuroleptic malignant syndrome, serotonin syndrome, and
tetanus. Before transfer, the patient continued to have episodes requiring escalating doses of
sedation ultimately leading to neuromuscular junction blockade to treat worsening
rhabdomyolysis. Upon arrival the patient’s neurologic examination off paralysis and sedation
was remarkable for following commands, intact cranial nerves, spontaneous movement of her
upper extremities (UE), but bilateral lower extremity (LE) rigidity with forced plantar
flexion. Tactile or auditory stimulation elicited episodes of reactive tachycardia, fever,
sweating, and hyperextension of her LE with normal UE tone. Initial work-up revealed only
rhabdomyolysis with associated acute kidney injury. MRI of the neuroaxis was
unremarkable, continuous EEG did not show evidence of seizure activity, and EMG showed
slow continuous firing in the absence of muscle activation. The patient’s clinical presentation
was consistent with SPS. Progressive antispasticity medications were added for symptomatic
control while immunomodulatory therapy for disease control was instituted. Her CSF
glutamic acid decarboxylase 65 antibody concentration was 124 nmol/L (nl < 0.02 nmol/L)
confirming our clinical diagnosis of SPS. After tracheostomy and PEG placement, the patient
was discharged to acute rehabilitation. She continues to follow-up at our facility for therapy
and is currently independently ambulatory on oral therapy. SPS necessitating ICU admission
is a rare event with limited descriptions in the literature.
